title: Clonal Hematopoiesis and Kidney Function in the ASPREE Cohort

sections.abstract:
Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is emerging as a novel risk factor for many nonhematological diseases. Although some studies suggest that CHIP is associated with adverse kidney outcomes, the results are conflicting across cohorts.

In this secondary analysis of the ASPirin in R educing E vents in the Elderly (ASPREE) trial, we assessed the association between CHIP and kidney function in 9434 community-dwelling adults aged > 70 years. At baseline, participants were free of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and major life-limiting illness. In addition, we performed meta-analysis of published cohorts investigating the association between CHIP and incident kidney function decline.

Of the participants, 2124 of 9434 (22.5%) had CHIP, of whom 532 had variant allele fraction (VAF) ≥ 10% and 887 had a single non- DNMT3A mutation. After adjusting for age and other confounders, there was no association between CHIP, including large CHIP or non- DNMT3A CHIP, and baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), baseline log-transformed urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), or rate of change of eGFR or log(UACR) over a median of 8.4 years of follow-up. Incident kidney function decline was not increased in this cohort, including in those with non- DNMT3A CHIP. Meta-analysis with other published cohorts supports an increased risk of incident kidney function decline in those with non- DNMT3A CHIP, with considerable heterogeneity.

We propose that the effect of CHIP is modified by participant factors, including comorbidities, partly accounting for heterogeneity across cohorts. This work contributes to a growing understanding of the interplay between CHIP and disease, and considerations in translating findings from large observational studies to individuals with CHIP.
sections.methods:
ASPREE was a 5-year randomized trial investigating whether low-dose aspirin, taken as primary prophylaxis, reduced disability-free survival in community dwelling older adults without known CVD or anemia. 12 The protocol and primary ASPREE results have been previously published. 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 Briefly, participants were enrolled in Australia and the USA but only Australian participants provided biobank samples 16 at baseline and could therefore be evaluated for baseline CHIP ( Supplementary Figure S2 ). In Australia, enrolled participants were community-dwelling adults aged > 70 years who did not have dementia, independence-limiting physical disability, CVD, anemia, or another condition limiting life expectancy to less than 5 years. Eligible individuals were recruited from March 2010 to December 2014 and randomized 1:1 to receive 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin daily or placebo. The intervention phase was terminated on June 12, 2017, and consenting participants continue to be followed as part of ASPREE-XT, an ongoing observational study. Follow-up includes annual visits with pathology, as well as collection of end point (adjudicated clinical event) data. Data up to and including the fourth annual visit after the intervention phase were used for this analysis.

CHIP status was determined in 9434 participants of the ASPREE-CHIP substudy using a custom-designed amplicon-based targeted sequencing assay. Additional details of the ASPREE trial and CHIP measurement are provided in the Supplementary Methods .

The presence of CHIP was defined at baseline as ≥ 1 mutation(s) in myeloid cancer–associated gene(s) present at VAF ≥ 2%. Participants with CHIP were further categorized as CHIP ≥ 10% if they had ≥1 variants with a VAF ≥ 10%, and as CHIP 2-10% if all detected CHIP variants were < 10%. For the categorical DNMT3A variable, CHIP participants were categorized as single DNMT3A if they had only 1 CHIP variant and the variant was in DNMT3A , single non- DNMT3A if they had 1 CHIP variant that was not in DNMT3A, and multiple mutations if they had > 1 CHIP variant.

Kidney function was assessed as either eGFR (estimated using the CKD-Epidemiology Collaboration 2021 creatinine equation 17 ) or the natural logarithm of UACR (lo[(UACR]). Incident kidney function decline was defined as ≥ 30% reduction in eGFR from baseline. A threshold of 30% rather than 50% was used because of the slower rate of progression of kidney impairment in the cohort. 18 Serum creatinine and UACR were measured at baseline and yearly thereafter including through the posttrial observational period.

We examined whether there was an association between CHIP and the following: (i) kidney function at baseline (using multivariable linear regression), (ii) change in kidney function over time (using mixed effects linear regression), and (iii) incident kidney function decline (using Cox proportional hazards regression). In addition, we performed random effects meta-analysis, pooling our results with published cohorts, to determine a pooled estimate for the risk of incident kidney function decline in people with CHIP.

In the multivariable linear regression and mixed effects regressions, primary analyses were performed with CHIP as a binary variable. Additional analyses were performed replacing the binary CHIP variable with a categorical variable based on VAF (no CHIP, CHIP 2-10%, and CHIP ≥10%) or DNMT3A status (no CHIP, single DNMT3A , single non- DNMT3A , multiple mutations). Adjustment covariates (age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, frailty, previous history of cancer) were selected based on known associations with CHIP and/or kidney function. 19 , 20 Covariate definitions are provided in the Supplementary Methods . For the outcome of eGFR, we included baseline log(UACR) as a covariate; and for the outcome of log(UACR), we included baseline eGFR as a covariate. We did not adjust for ethnicity because 99% of participants were White or Caucasian. Fewer than 10% of participants had missing outcome measures or covariates at baseline (most commonly baseline UACR, Supplementary Table S1 ) and were excluded from the models.

Mixed effects linear regression was used to model kidney function over time. This method allowed for correlation among repeated measures from the same individual by including a random intercept and slope for the individual. The models included CHIP, time, and fixed covariates as in the multivariable linear regression, as well as random (participant-specific) intercept and slope terms. The effect of CHIP on the rate of change of kidney function was assessed with a CHIP-time interaction term. To assess the effect of VAF and gene on the rate of change of kidney function, we used the respective categorical CHIP variables in the mixed effects models and performed a likelihood ratio test to see if model fit was improved with a CHIP-time interaction term. A nonsignificant P -value for the likelihood ratio test was interpreted as no evidence of a relationship between VAF or DNMT3A mutation status and kidney function decline.

The number of participants contributing kidney function measures at each time point is shown in Supplementary Table S2 . For the primary analysis, we excluded the final time point (year 11) because few participants had measures at this time point. We performed a sensitivity analysis including only the first 7 years of follow-up. We also performed a sensitivity analysis using generalized estimating equations, rather than mixed effects linear regression, specifying an exchangeable correlation structure, analogous to a random intercept. To determine whether any potential associations of CHIP would be detectable only in people with established CKD, we repeated the multivariable linear regression and mixed effects linear regressions restricted to those with eGFR < 60 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 at baseline.

Cox proportional hazards regression was used to model the association between CHIP and incident kidney function decline, with death considered as a competing risk. We excluded those with missing adjustment covariates, missing baseline eGFR or no follow-up eGFR. Separate analyses were performed for the binary CHIP variable and for the categorical CHIP variable based on DNMT3A status. Adjustment covariates were age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, frailty, previous history of cancer, baseline eGFR, and baseline log(UACR). Participants were censored at the time of death or loss to follow-up. Random effects meta-analyses were used to pool results from our cohort and other cohorts where the risk of incident kidney function decline was reported. All analyses were performed in Stata v17. 21
sections.results:
At baseline, the median age of participants was 73.7 years and 54% were female, with diabetes and hypertension present in 10% and 74%, respectively ( Table 1 ). Of the 9434 participants sequenced, 2124 (22.5%) had CHIP: 1592 with VAF 2-10% and 532 with VAF ≥ 10%. The most common mutations were in DNMT3A , TET2 , and ASXL1 ( Supplementary Figure S3 and Table S3 ). Of the participants with CHIP, 1808 (85%) had a single mutation, of which 921 (51%) were in DNMT3A and 887 (49%) were in a gene other than DNMT3A . There were 259 CHIP participants (12%) with 2 mutations, and 54 (3%) with 3. The median VAF was 5.1% (interquartile range [IQR]: 3.0–9.1). At baseline, the median eGFR was 79 ml/min per 1.73m 2 (IQR: 68–89), median UACR was 0.8 mg/mmol (IQR: 0.5–1.4); 12% had eGFR < 60 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 and 10.5% had albuminuria. Both small (2-10% VAF) and large (≥ 10% VAF) clones, as well as DNMT3A and non- DNTM3A CHIP were associated with baseline eGFR in unadjusted models ( Supplementary Table S4 ). Over a median follow-up of 8.4 years, participants had a median of 8 (IQR: 7–9) eGFR measurements and 7 (IQR: 4–8) UACR measurements. Overall, eGFR declined by 1.0 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 /yr, and this did not differ for those with or without CHIP ( P = 0.56) ( Table 3 , Figure 1 ). Log(UACR) increased by 0.074 log(mg/mmol)/yr, and there was no difference between participants with and without CHIP ( P = 0.68). We found no suggestion that VAF ≥ 10% or non- DNMT3A mutations were associated with either measure of kidney function ( Table 3 ). Additional analyses were performed to verify the robustness of these findings. First, we confirmed that statistically significant differences in rate of change of eGFR and log(UACR) could be detected in this cohort in those with diabetes or hypertension at baseline ( Supplementary Table S5 ). Second, given that it may be expected that there is skewing of the kidney function over time because participants with more health issues are more likely to drop out, we performed a sensitivity analysis limiting follow-up to 7 years and observed little difference in the estimates ( Supplementary Table S6 ). Finally, we modelled kidney function decline using generalized estimating equations rather than the mixed effects model and observed similar results ( Supplementary Table S7 ).

Considering that previous studies had shown associations between CHIP and kidney function decline in those with preexisting CKD ( Supplementary Figure S1 ), we performed additional analyses restricted to those with eGFR < 60 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 at baseline ( n = 1101). In this subgroup, the median eGFR was 54 ml/min (IQR: 48–57), and median UACR was 1.0 mg/mmol (IQR: 0.5–2.0) ( Supplementary Tables S8 and S9 ). Among participants with baseline eGFR < 60ml/min, the mean eGFR was slightly lower, by 1.04 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ( P = 0.04), in those with CHIP in the fully adjusted analysis ( Supplementary Table S10 ). However, mean log(UACR) was not statistically different, and rates of decline of both eGFR or log(UACR) were similar with or without CHIP ( Supplementary Table S11 ).

Next, we considered a binary outcome of incident 30% decline in kidney function. This occurred in 1249 of 6716 (19%) of participants without CHIP and 402 of 1934 (21%) of participants with CHIP, of whom 173 of 847 (20%) were participants with single DNMT3A -CHIP, 155 of 802 (19%) were those with single non- DNMT3A -CHIP, and 74 of 285 (26%) were those with multiple mutations. After adjusting for age and other potential confounders, there was no association between CHIP and incident kidney function decline (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.11 [0.99–1.24]). There was no association between either DNMT3A (HR: 1.09 [0.93–1.28] or non- DNMT3A CHIP (HR: 1.03 [0.88–1.22]) and incident kidney function decline; however, there was an increased risk of incident kidney function decline in those with multiple mutations (HR: 1.38 [1.09–1.75]).

We searched the literature for studies investigating an association between kidney function and CHIP ( Supplementary Figure S1 and Table S12 ). Studies were eligible if they reported a risk measure (odds ratio or HR) adjusted for age with or without other confounder adjustment. Abstract proceedings were excluded. From the eligible studies, we identified 5 studies, including 11 nonoverlapping cohorts, that evaluated the outcome of incident kidney function decline in individuals with CHIP compared with those without CHIP. Of these, 3 studies (comprising 8 cohorts) reported risk for individuals with DNMT3A- and non- DNMT3A CHIP. None of the studies reported outcomes for people with multiple CHIP mutations. The studies ranged in size from 85 to 8650 participants, and included population-based cohorts, as well as cohorts selecting participants with CKD, or diabetes. Incident kidney function decline was most commonly defined as ≥ 30% or ≥ 50% decline in eGFR ( Supplementary Table S12 ). Visual inspection of contour enhanced funnel plots did not suggest publication bias.

We performed random effects meta-analysis to pool our results with those of previous studies ( Figure 2 ). On meta-analysis, there was an association with incident kidney function decline in those with CHIP (HR: 1.16 [1.01–1.34] and this was restricted to those with non- DNMT3A CHIP (HR: 1.39 [1.01–1.90]) rather than DNMT3A CHIP (HR: 1.05 [0.94–1.17]). There was considerable heterogeneity in estimates for incident kidney decline in those with CHIP ( I 2 = 52%) or non- DNMT3A CHIP ( I 2 = 85%). sections.discussion:
In this large and well-characterized cohort of community-dwelling older adults with annual assessment of both eGFR and UACR, we found no statistically significant difference in either baseline kidney function or decline in kidney function over a median follow-up of 8.4 years, in those with or without CHIP, including those with non- DN M T 3A CHIP. In addition, in this cohort, CHIP was not associated with greater risk of a 30% decline in kidney function, except in those with multiple mutations. Although meta-analysis of our findings with published cohorts supported an increased risk of incident kidney function decline in non- DNMT3A CHIP, we demonstrated considerable variability in risk estimates across cohorts.

There are several possible reasons for the conflicting reports of the association between CHIP and kidney function. First, cross-sectional associations, or those with minimal adjustment factors, may reflect unmeasured confounding. For example, factors associated with inflammation could potentially lead to both increased CHIP prevalence and decreased kidney function. Second, misclassification bias may be present. This may explain why some longitudinal studies have reported an association between CHIP and incident kidney function decline defined as a binary variable (e.g., % reduction in eGFR) ( Supplementary Figure S1 ), but found no difference in the rate of change of eGFR between those with and those without CHIP. 4 , 5 , 10 Similarly, we found that those with > 1 mutation had an increased risk of incident kidney function decline, but no difference in the rate of change eGFR or log(UACR), although the number of participants was small. Third, participant characteristics may influence the association between CHIP and kidney function decline. Such an association has predominantly been reported in people with underlying CKD. In contrast, among otherwise healthy participants without major life-limiting comorbidities, such as those enrolled in ASPREE, the impact of CHIP may be much less than in those with other additive risk factors or higher baseline levels of inflammation. Unlike other CKD cohorts, 4 , 5 even the subgroup of ASPREE participants with baseline eGFR < 60 ml/min, had low levels of albuminuria and relatively low prevalence of comorbidities such as diabetes.

In support of the idea that CHIP interacts with other risk factors, initial risk estimates for CHIP and atherosclerotic CVD from case-control studies or high-risk cohorts suggested a 2 to 4–fold increased risk of CVD 22 , 23 ; whereas studies in population-based cohorts have shown a more modest effect. 3 , 24 , 25 , 26 Seminal work on the link between CHIP and CVD demonstrated that Tet2 -deficient, low-density lipoprotein–receptor-deficient mice that were fed a high-fat diet had accelerated atherosclerosis. However, the same mice did not develop atherosclerosis when fed a normal diet, despite their Tet2 deficiency. 27 Similarly, Bhattacharya et al. 28 found that only individuals with CHIP who had unhealthy diet had increased risk of cardiovascular events, whereas those with CHIP and healthy diet had no increased risk. In addition, in a Korean cohort, CHIP was shown to have a synergistic effect with high low-density lipoprotein levels to increase the risk of atherosclerotic CVD. 29 It is therefore plausible that CHIP alone is insufficient to cause kidney damage; and in an otherwise healthy cohort, such as that studied here, CHIP has little impact on decline in kidney function.

A limitation of this analysis is that across the cohort there was little change in kidney function over time, likely reflecting the general health of the participants, which may have limited our power to detect differences. Nevertheless, we were able to detect statistically significant differences in the rate of decline in kidney function in participants with diabetes or hypertension in this cohort. Similarly, although participant drop out can lead to positive skewing of kidney function over time, an analysis limiting our follow-up to 7 years showed similar results. Subgroup analyses were limited by relatively small numbers; however, the narrow confidence intervals indicate that the effect of CHIP on rate of kidney decline, if present, would still be minimal, and certainly less than the effect of established comorbidities such as diabetes or hypertension. Strengths of our analysis are that this is the largest cohort of older adults with serial measurements of both eGFR and UACR. Furthermore, we were able to comprehensively adjust for factors associated with CKD, including frailty.

Our study contributes to the growing understanding of CHIP and supports the hypothesis that the impact of CHIP differs based on participant characteristics. These nuances are important to understand further to allow individualized counselling for people who may be incidentally found to have CHIP, and to better understand how CHIP causes disease.
